canonicalName: Group theory from the solution of polynomial equations (abstract groups)

evidence.claim: Cayley's Philosophical Magazine paper on the theory of groups, depending on the symbolic equation theta^n=1, is indexed as 1854
MacTutor reports that Cayley's definition uses closure, associativity and inverses without tying the group to permutations; Galois's own group work reached print only in 1846
Galois's collected mathematical works first appeared in Liouville's journal in 1846 (pp. 381-444)

conceptual.note: Read as the first public statement of the group as an object independent of permutations. Earlier public uses of permutation groups without abstraction: Ruffini 1799 (book), Abel 1826 (Crelle), Cauchy's 1815 papers (not checked), Galois 1846. Lagrange's 1770s Reflexions (not located in a bibliographic record) is often cited as the precursor; MacTutor says groups appear there only in hindsight. Priority dispute: abstract definition is also credited to Dyck 1882 and Weber 1882/1893, who gave finite abstract definitions; Cayley's 1854 paper was little noticed until the 1870s (not verified here).

evidence.claim: Ruffini's 1799 book Teoria generale delle equazioni argues the general quintic cannot be solved by radicals
MacTutor says Ruffini used group theory in that work, introducing order, conjugacy and cycle decomposition of permutation groups
Abel's 1826 Crelle paper gives a proof that the general equation of degree above four is unsolvable by radicals

methodological.note: First purposeful use of permutation groups on solvability of equations. MacTutor notes Ruffini's proof has a gap; Abel 1824 (pamphlet, not located) and 1826 completed it. Galois's criterion (solvability iff solvable group) was written c. 1830-32 and printed only in 1846, so the criterion's publication date is 1846.

evidence.claim: Earliest title found naming a theory of groups: Cayley 1854
Jordan's Traite des substitutions et des equations algebriques (1870) is the first major group-theory treatise per MacTutor
Burnside's Theory of groups of finite order is indexed as 1897 (first English textbook-style title)

institutional.note: Earliest indexed title found, not an absolute claim; searched Crossref and zbMATH only. Jordan 1870 (treatise), Netto 1882 (Substitutionentheorie, not located in a record), Burnside 1897 are the textbook milestones.

canonicalName: Non-Euclidean (hyperbolic) geometry and the independence of the parallel postulate

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Lobachevsky's 1829 piece in the Kazan Messenger is the first account of non-Euclidean geometry to appear in print
MacTutor topic page dates Lobachevsky's work to 1829 and his clearest account (Geometrische Untersuchungen) to 1840

conceptual.note: Publication year governs. Private earlier: Gauss believed the fifth postulate independent by about 1817 (MacTutor), with letters to Gerling, Schumacher and Farkas Bolyai; Janos Bolyai wrote to his father in 1823 of his discoveries. Bolyai's Appendix to the Tentamen appeared about 1832 (zbMATH has only 1902/1909 reprints; the original year not verified here). Precursors exploring denials: Saccheri (Euclides vindicatus, 1733) and Lambert (1766 per MacTutor, printed later); neither accepted the denial as consistent.

evidence.claim: Beltrami, Saggio di interpretazione della geometria non-euclidea (1868), indexed in zbMATH
MacTutor: Beltrami was the first to place Bolyai-Lobachevsky geometry on the same footing as Euclidean; Klein completed the model in 1871

methodological.note: Reads 'first purposeful application' as the first model that establishes relative consistency, hence independence of the postulate. Lobachevsky's 1829-1840 development itself (analytic trigonometry) is the earlier constructive use, see conceptual.

evidence.claim: Klein, Ueber die sogenannte Nicht-Euklidische Geometrie, Math. Ann. 4 (1871)
zbMATH lists Klein's 1871 paper and its 1873 sequel under the same title

institutional.note: Earliest indexed title found naming Nicht-Euklidische Geometrie (Crossref and zbMATH 1800-1880). Lobachevsky 1837 'Geometrie imaginaire' (Crelle, zbMATH 2751213) and 1840 'Geometrische Untersuchungen zur Theorie der Parallellinien' are earlier titles naming the topic differently.

canonicalName: Differential equations from the calculus (ordinary differential equations as a subject)

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Jacob Bernoulli's May 1690 Acta Eruditorum paper reduced the isochrone problem to a first-order nonlinear differential equation and solved it by separating variables

conceptual.note: Earliest published solution of a differential equation I could evidence. Newton's De methodis serierum et fluxionum was written in 1671 but first printed in English in 1736 (MacTutor, Newton), so private priority is earlier. Leibniz's 1684 calculus paper (Acta Eruditorum) is not a differential-equation paper and I found no bibliographic record for it. No Crossref/zbMATH records exist for 1690.

evidence.claim: Same MacTutor account: the isochrone equation was solved by what is now called separation of variables

methodological.note: Treated as the same event as conceptual because the first public statement and its solution coincide. Evidence rests on one secondary page; the primary Acta Eruditorum item was not located.

evidence.claim: Euler's Nova methodus innumerabiles aequationes differentiales secundi gradus reducendi, written 1728, published in Comm. Acad. Sci. Petropol. 3 (1732)

Searched archive.org, zbMATH, Euler Archive only. Euler's calculus textbook of 1768-70 dedicates much of it to differential equations (content not verified).

canonicalName: Positive Grassmannian as a hub (total positivity, ASEP, KP solitons)

evidence.claim: Postnikov, Total positivity, Grassmannians, and networks, arXiv 27 Sep 2006
zbMATH record of the same preprint (2006)

conceptual.note: Cell structure and counting of the totally nonnegative Grassmannian is published by Williams 2005, with Postnikov 2006 the systematic account; Lusztig's Total positivity in reductive groups (Lie Theory and Geometry, 1994, doi 10.1007/978-1-4612-0261-5_20) introduced total positivity for flag-type spaces earlier. Which counts as 'the idea' is a judgement; the hub (ASEP and KP) idea is later. Postnikov's preprint has no journal record found.
